hints: Start by writing the general pattern for any reaction change as sum for products minus sum for reactants, remembering to multiply each table value by its balancing number in reaction 1.
Recall that $\Delta H^\ominus$ comes from $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values and $\Delta S^\ominus$ comes from $S^\ominus$ values, and note that $\text{O}_2(\text{g})$ has $\Delta H_f^\ominus = 0$.
Think about how to link $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ to $\Delta G^\ominus$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$, checking that temperature is in kelvin and energy units match in kJ.
walkthrough:
Find the entropy change from absolute entropies**
Think of entropy change as what you finish with minus what you started with. For reaction 1, $\text{CS}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{SO}_2(\text{g})$, so you multiply each $S^\ominus$ by its coefficient. That gives: $$\Delta S^\ominus = [S^\ominus(\text{CO}_2) + 2S^\ominus(\text{SO}_2)] - [S^\ominus(\text{CS}_2) + 3S^\ominus(\text{O}_2)]$$ Substituting: $$(213.8 + 2 \times 248.2) - (237.8 + 3 \times 205.2) = -143.2 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign makes sense because 4 moles of gas become 3 moles of gas, so disorder decreases.

Find the enthalpy change from formation data**
Use exactly the same products minus reactants idea, but now with $\Delta H_f^\ominus$. Remember an element in its standard state like $\text{O}_2(\text{g})$ has zero enthalpy of formation, but you still include its coefficient for entropy. $$\Delta H^\ominus = [\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{CO}_2) + 2\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{SO}_2)] - [\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{CS}_2)]$$ Substituting: $$(-393.5 + 2 \times -296.8) - (116.7) = -1103.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ This large negative value tells you combustion is strongly exothermic.

Combine them with the Gibbs equation**
Free energy brings enthalpy and entropy together: $$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$$ First convert $25^\circ\text{C}$ to kelvin: $T = 25 + 273 = 298 \text{ K}$. Then the classic trap is units. $\Delta H^\ominus$ is in kJ but $\Delta S^\ominus$ is in J, so divide by 1000: $-143.2 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} = -0.1432 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$. Now substitute: $$\Delta G^\ominus = -1103.8 - (298 \times -0.1432) = -1103.8 + 42.67 = -1061.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ A very negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ means reaction 1 is highly feasible.

hints: Recall that a reaction is feasible when $\Delta G^\ominus$ is negative or zero, so the maximum temperature for feasibility occurs at the boundary where $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$.

Rearrange $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ to $T = \Delta H^\ominus / \Delta S^\ominus$ and check that both $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ are in consistent energy units before dividing.
walkthrough:
Picture what maximum temperature means**
Here both $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ are negative. At low temperature the exothermic enthalpy term wins and $\Delta G^\ominus$ is negative. As temperature rises, the $-T\Delta S^\ominus$ term becomes more positive and eventually $\Delta G^\ominus$ turns positive. The crossover point is where: $$\Delta G^\ominus = 0$$ That is the highest temperature at which the reaction can still be feasible.

Rearrange and calculate with matching units**
Starting from: $$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$$ Set to zero and rearrange: $$T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$$ Convert $\Delta S^\ominus = -365.5 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} = -0.3655 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ to match $\Delta H^\ominus = -261.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Then: $$T = \frac{-261.6}{-0.3655} = 715.7 \text{ K}$$ So about $716 \text{ K}$. Above this temperature $\Delta G^\ominus$ becomes positive and the reaction is no longer feasible.

Final answer: At boundary, $\Delta G^\ominus = 0$, so $T = \Delta H^\ominus / \Delta S^\ominus$
$T = -261.6 / -0.3655 = 715.7 \text{ K}$
